chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Math of Portfolio Construction

lessons.title: Building a Simple Return Simulation for Your Angel Portfolio

body.text: An expected MOIC is an average across thousands of hypothetical universes where you ran the same portfolio again and again. You only get to run it once, with real money, and the universe you actually land in can look very different from the average.

children.text: Every calculation so far in this course has produced a single number, an expected multiple, an expected IRR. Those numbers are real and useful, but they hide something important: even if your assumptions about hit rates and outcomes are exactly right, the actual portfolio you end up holding is a random draw, and that draw has a wide spread of possible results. This lesson builds a simple simulation to show you that spread, using the same illustrative 20-position portfolio from Chapter 1.

Simplify the Lesson 1.1 outcome table into two states, to make the simulation tractable by hand. Of the 90% of positions that are not a genuine 10x-plus hit (the 0x, 1x and 3x buckets), the average multiple works out to (50 × 0 + 25 × 1 + 15 × 3) ÷ 90 = 0.78x. Of the 10% that do clear 10x, blending the 5% at 10x and 5% at 50x, the average multiple is (5 × 10 + 5 × 50) ÷ 10 = 30x. That gives a clean two-state model: any given position has a 90% chance of averaging 0.78x, and a 10% chance of averaging 30x.

The number of 10x-plus hits in a 20-position portfolio, at a 10% hit rate, follows a binomial distribution, the same mathematics behind Lesson 1.2's shots-on-goal probability. This table extends that math from just "at least one hit" to the full distribution of exactly how many hits a portfolio might realistically land, and what portfolio MOIC each of those outcomes actually produces.

body.label: The Uncomfortable Truth in Row One
body.context: Even with sound underwriting, correctly estimated probabilities, and a well-built 20-position portfolio, roughly 1 in 8 outcomes is a portfolio with no genuine 10x-plus winner at all.

body.text: The expected MOIC of 3.70x exactly matches the MOIC produced by landing precisely 2 hits, the single most probable outcome in the table. That is not a coincidence: because portfolio MOIC is a linear function of the number of hits, the expected MOIC always equals the MOIC you would get from exactly the expected number of hits (20 positions × 10% = 2 hits here). The catch is that you do not get the expected number of hits, you get some specific whole number, and the table shows how much that number can vary.

Two angels can run identical underwriting processes, make equally sound decisions, and still end up with visibly different track records purely because one landed in the 12.2% zero-hit outcome and the other landed in the 28.5% two-hit outcome. A single realised portfolio is a very small sample. Do not read too much into one angel's, including your own, first full portfolio cycle as proof of skill or its absence.

children.text: More Positions Narrows the Spread, It Doesn't Guarantee the Average

Lesson 1.2 showed that more positions raise the probability of catching at least one hit. The same breadth also shrinks the probability of the worst-case zero-hit outcome, which is really the same binomial math viewed from a different angle. At 20 positions and a 10% hit rate, the chance of zero hits is 12.2%. Push the same assumptions out to 30 positions and that falls to about 4.2%, nearly a threefold reduction, without changing the hit rate at all.

body.title: Confirm the Variance-Reduction Effect
body.prompt: At a 10% per-position hit rate, what is the probability of ending up with zero hits at all in a 30-position portfolio? Answer in percent, e.g. 10.0 for 10.0%.
body.explanation: P(zero hits) = (1 − 0.10)^30 = 0.9^30 ≈ 0.0424, or about 4.2%. Compare this to the 12.2% at 20 positions: adding 10 more positions to the portfolio nearly triples the odds of avoiding the worst-case outcome, even though it does not change the expected MOIC at all.

children.text: What This Simple Model Still Leaves Out: Correlation

Binomial math assumes every position's outcome is independent of every other position's, a coin flip that does not know or care what the other coins landed on. Real startups are not that independent. A funding winter, a sector-wide valuation reset, or a macro downturn can push failure probabilities up across many positions in the same portfolio at once, especially ones raised in the same year or concentrated in the same sector. When outcomes are correlated instead of independent, the real spread of possible portfolio results is wider than this clean model suggests, with a fatter tail on the downside. Chapter 3 covers sector, stage, and geography diversification, and Chapter 5 covers spreading investments across time (vintage diversification), specifically to manage this correlation risk that a simple binomial model cannot see.

body.title: Run Your Own Monte Carlo Simulation

children.text: For a more realistic picture than the hand-built table above, simulate thousands of random portfolios drawn from the full five-outcome distribution in Lesson 1.1, rather than the simplified two-state version, and look at the spread of resulting MOICs.

content.code:
import random

def simulate_portfolio(n_positions=20, n_trials=20000):
    # (probability, return multiple) pairs, matching Lesson 1.1's table
    outcomes = [(0.50, 0), (0.25, 1), (0.15, 3), (0.05, 10), (0.05, 50)]
    results = []
    for _ in range(n_trials):
        total_multiple = 0
        for _ in range(n_positions):
            r = random.random()
            cumulative = 0
            for prob, multiple in outcomes:
                cumulative += prob
                if r <= cumulative:
                    total_multiple += multiple
                    break
        results.append(total_multiple / n_positions)
    results.sort()
    return results

results = simulate_portfolio()
n = len(results)
print('P10:', results[int(0.10 * n)])
print('Median:', results[int(0.50 * n)])
print('Mean:', sum(results) / n)
print('P90:', results[int(0.90 * n)])
content.caption: Running this typically shows a median MOIC noticeably below the mean, since a handful of high-multiple simulated draws pull the average up, the same skew you would expect from a power-law process.

body.title: Two Angels, Two Very Different Track Records
body.scenario: Angel A built a 20-position portfolio in 2020 and ended up with a 3.70x MOIC. Angel B, a friend who used what looks like the same diligence process and the same rough hit-rate assumptions, built their own 20-position portfolio the same year and ended up with a 0.78x MOIC.
body.prompt: What should you actually conclude about Angel A's and Angel B's relative skill from this?
body.modelAnswer: Very little, at least not from this alone. Angel A landed in the most probable single outcome (2 hits, 28.5% probability). Angel B's 0.78x outcome corresponds to zero hits, which this lesson's own table shows had roughly a 12.2% probability even under sound, correctly calibrated assumptions. One realised portfolio per angel is a sample size of one, and the spread in this lesson's table shows that gap is well within what pure variance can produce between two equally sound processes. To actually compare skill, you would want to look at the quality of each angel's underwriting process and diligence depth, and ideally compare results across several portfolio vintages rather than a single one, since variance averages out over repeated cycles in a way it cannot within just one.

points: Expected MOIC is an average across many hypothetical portfolios; the one portfolio you actually build is a single random draw from a wide distribution of possible outcomes
At a 10% hit rate and 20 positions, roughly 1 in 8 well-built portfolios will still land with zero genuine 10x-plus hits, purely by chance

Expected MOIC always equals the MOIC produced by exactly the expected number of hits, because portfolio MOIC is a linear function of hit count, even though you never actually land on a fractional number of hits
Adding more positions narrows the spread of likely outcomes and shrinks the odds of the worst case, without changing the expected MOIC itself

This simple model assumes independent outcomes; real correlation across a vintage or sector widens the true spread beyond what plain binomial math shows, which is exactly what Chapters 3 and 5 address
